name: Liebfrauenkirche Kitzbühel
kurzbeschreibung: The Liebfrauenkirche Kitzbühel impresses with its 48 m fortified tower, the famous 6.4-tonne 'Kaiserglocke' from 1845, and masterly Baroque art.
oeffnungszeiten: Ganzjährig tagsüber tgl. ca. 08:00–18:00 Uhr geöffnet
beschreibung:
Overview

Steeped in history, the Liebfrauenkirche is picturesquely perched on the wooded church hill directly north of Kitzbühel's historic old town. Together with the neighboring parish church of St. Andreas and the cemetery adorned with ornate wrought-iron grave crosses, the ensemble forms the unmistakable architectural landmark of the legendary chamois town of Kitzbühel. Originally erected in the 14th century as a two-storey Gothic cemetery chapel housing a charnel house (ossuary), the church was crowned in the 16th century with a monumental 48-metre-high bell tower that dominates the town's chime to this day.

Architectural History, Baroque Transformation & the Kaiserglocke

The church was first documented in 1373. For centuries, the lower level served as a charnel house (ossuary) holding the remains of deceased Kitzbühel citizens. The monument owes its distinctive exterior appearance—a massive defensive tower perched upon a comparatively delicate chapel—to a structural necessity: around 1518, when the town of Kitzbühel purchased a massive new bell, the slender Romanesque tower of the adjacent parish church proved structurally inadequate. Consequently, between 1566 and 1569, master builder Wilhelm Egarter erected the 48-metre fortified tower on top of the Liebfrauenkirche, complete with battlements and a Baroque belfry dome, to serve as the town's principal bell tower. In the 18th century, the upper chapel underwent a splendid Baroque transformation: sculptor Jakob Singer, stucco artist Hans Singer, and painter Simon Benedikt Faistenberger created vibrant ceiling stucco and frescoes; the magnificent high altar from 1702 enshrines a deeply venerated Mariahilf pilgrimage painting. The crowning glory of the belfry is the legendary Kaiserglocke: cast in 1845 by Josef Georg Miller in Innsbruck, this bronze colossus weighs a staggering 6,374 kilograms (with a diameter of almost two metres). Originally commissioned for the Innsbruck Cathedral, it was diverted to Kitzbühel following a minor casting flaw. During the First World War, when it was requisitioned to be melted down for munitions, an imperial petition from the local citizenry saved the bell from destruction. Today, it is revered as one of the most melodious and resounding bells in all of Tyrol.

Visit & Getting There

The Liebfrauenkirche is freely accessible free of charge daily year-round from approximately 08:00 to 18:00 (during church services and devotions, sightseeing should be conducted with discretion). Getting there: from the Kitzbühel Vorderstadt, it is just a pleasant five-minute stroll across the Kirchplatz up onto the church hill. By train: take ÖBB trains to Bahnhof Kitzbühel Hahnenkamm, followed by a 7-minute walk. By car: via the B161 into Kitzbühel; public parking is available at the Pfarrau parking area or in the town centre.

Tips

The cemetery grounds and the approach to the church forecourt feature paved, low-barrier paths; the interior of the upper church is accessible without steps. If you happen to visit Kitzbühel during major ecclesiastical holidays (such as Easter, Corpus Christi, or Assumption Day), ascend the hill at noon to experience the incomparably deep, solemn resonance of the Kaiserglocke tolling across the valley.
